hello.note: Formal greeting; reply is Misawa ahinya. Casually, peers say Ber (reply Ber ahinya).

good_morning.note: Literally 'has it opened?' (the sky); reply Oyawore ahinya.

good_evening.note: Literally 'has it closed?'; reply Owimore ahinya.

how_are_you.note: Literally 'how do you fare?'; reply Ber ahinya, to in? (well, and you?).

thank_you.note: Erokamano ahinya is 'thank you very much'.

youre_welcome.note: Literally 'there's no matter'; the standard reply to erokamano. Glosbe confirms this pairing directly. Rejected rival: machiegni is what GT gives, but it back-translates as the greeting 'welcome' (as to an arriving guest), not the reply-to-thanks sense, so it's a false friend here.

no_problem.note: Literally 'there's no bad(ness)'; casual reassurance, distinct from onge wach. Rach ('bad/wrong') is independently confirmed on Glosbe and this phrase is a stable dictionary-tier GT entry both directions. Rejected rival: the earlier pick onge chandruok was built from a single machine-translated sentence and chandruok has no independent confirmation anywhere checked.

excuse_me.note: Literally 'do me a kindness'; Omniglot confirms it for getting someone's attention, and the same phrase covers asking forgiveness.

no.note: Tawe is a common regional variant; both are per Omniglot's phrasebook. GT instead gives ooyo as a stable dictionary-tier entry, but Omniglot (the more native-vetted source) lists only dawe/tawe, so dawe is preferred here; ooyo is noted as a possible alternate form.

of_course.note: Literally 'truly, really', confirmed standalone on Glosbe; used as a firm, certain yes. Rejected rival: GT's donge has no independent confirmation (no Glosbe entry, and reverse-translates as 'might', not 'of course'), so the plainer, better-attested adier is kept.

amazing.note: Literally 'very good!'; a well-attested, all-purpose exclamation of enthusiasm. Rejected rivals: gima lich and GT's makelo wuoro/malich all rely on lich/wuoro roots whose meaning is inconsistent across sources (malich round-trips as 'Major', not 'wonderful'), so the plainer ber ahinya is preferred over an unconfirmed 'amazing'-specific word.

cheers.note: Literally 'good life/good health'; ngima and maber are each independently confirmed words, but no source checked (Omniglot lists the toast category with no entry) confirms a fixed Dholuo drinking-toast idiom, so treat this as a plausible wish rather than an attested toast.
